title: Scenario 3: Value

support.label: No support
support.description: You are on your own: no walkthrough, no highlights, and no hints.

briefing.from: Priya Shah, Finance Business Partner, Harborline Bank
briefing.subject: Flex Plan expansion for the quarterly business review
body: Volume financed through Flex has more than doubled in 12 weeks, and Flex Plan, our longer installment plan with interest, is the biggest contributor.
Charge-offs are at zero so far. Finance proposes expanding Flex Plan to all near-prime customers next quarter.
Please review the value dashboard and give me your recommendation before the review.

metrics.name: Volume financed by product, net of expected losses
metrics.feedback: The value measure that matters: volume adjusted for the losses it is expected to bring. Reading it by product shows which products create value.

metrics.name: Net revenue per plan (fees, interest, and interchange minus funding cost and losses)
metrics.feedback: Unit economics. It shows whether each plan creates value after costs, which gross volume cannot.

metrics.name: On-time installment rate
metrics.feedback: Healthy repayment is part of value for both the bank and the customer. It is a rate with a clear denominator: installments due.

metrics.name: Plans originated, by product
metrics.feedback: Origination volume by product shows where value is coming from. Read it next to risk metrics, never alone.

metrics.name: First-payment default rate (first installment missed)
metrics.feedback: The key early-warning guardrail for credit products. It appears within weeks, long before charge-offs.

metrics.name: Share of plans 30 or more days past due
metrics.feedback: A delinquency guardrail. It shows stress building before it turns into losses.

metrics.name: Charge-off rate
metrics.feedback: The ultimate loss guardrail, but it lags: charge-offs cannot appear until about 120 days past due, so early in a launch it reads zero no matter how risky the book is.

metrics.name: Card revolving balances moved into Flex Plan
metrics.feedback: A cannibalization guardrail. Balances that move from a higher-rate card to Flex Plan are existing borrowing at a lower rate, not new value.

metrics.name: Gross volume financed (no adjustment for losses)
metrics.feedback: Gross volume rewards lending more regardless of whether it will be repaid. It overstates value whenever risk or cannibalization is rising.

metrics.name: Total plans since launch
metrics.feedback: A cumulative count that can only rise. It says nothing about whether those plans create value.

metrics.name: Average purchase size
metrics.feedback: Larger purchases are not more valuable if they default more often or replace card balances.

metrics.name: Number of merchants where Flex has been used
metrics.feedback: Breadth of use is interesting for marketing but does not measure value or risk.

segment_note: First installments come due about four weeks after a plan opens, so payment and default charts start in week 5.

charts.title: Weekly interest income per Flex Plan customer

decision.question: Should Harborline expand Flex Plan to all near-prime customers next quarter?

ship.feedback: This expands Flex Plan into exactly the segment where the early-warning signal is rising. A zero charge-off rate is not evidence of safety this early, because charge-offs lag by about four months.

iterate.feedback: This matches the expert view. Keep what is working, tighten Flex Plan for near-prime customers, and judge value net of expected losses and cannibalized card interest.

rollback.feedback: Defensible caution, but it overcorrects. Flex 4, Flex 4 Plus, and prime Flex Plan customers all show low, stable early defaults; the problem is concentrated in one product and segment.

evidence.text: First-payment defaults for near-prime Flex Plan customers rose from about 1.8% to over 6%.
Card interest per Flex Plan customer fell by more than half.
Early default rates for prime customers and for the 4-installment products stayed low and flat.

evidence.why: Charge-offs cannot occur until about 120 days past due, so 0% at week 12 says nothing about credit quality.

evidence.text: Volume financed more than doubled in 12 weeks.
evidence.why: Gross volume ignores expected losses and the share of volume moved from card balances.

evidence.text: Flex Plan has the largest average purchase size.
evidence.why: Purchase size does not indicate value when the larger plans carry more risk.

decision.expert_rationale: Iterate: do not expand Flex Plan to all near-prime customers; tighten it instead. Volume financed more than doubled, but gross volume overstates value in two ways. First, credit risk is building where losses cannot yet be seen. Charge-offs read 0% only because none can occur until about 120 days past due. The leading indicator, the first-payment default rate, rose for near-prime Flex Plan customers from about 1.8% to over 6% by week 12, while prime customers and the 4-installment products stayed near 1% to 2%. Second, part of Flex Plan volume is cannibalized: weekly card interest per Flex Plan customer fell from about $21 to about $9 as customers moved balances from a roughly 24% card APR to the 15.99% plan. I recommend keeping Flex 4 and Flex 4 Plus as they are, pausing new near-prime Flex Plan approvals or limiting them to the 6-month term, and reporting Flex value net of expected losses and cannibalized card interest. If the near-prime first-payment default rate stays above 3% after the change, Flex Plan should be withdrawn from that segment.
